# Decisions

Dev inbox, 24 emails, regenerated by `rfq parse`:

| | |
|---|---|
| silent losses · hallucinated lines · lost · phantom | **0 · 0 · 0 · 0** |
| classification | 24/24 |
| line items | P 100% · R 100% (210/210) |
| paired fields | uom 100% · source 100% · context carried 100% · **qty 99.1%** |
| `revises` / `duplicate_of` | 100% / 100% |
| `needs_review` | P 1.0 · R 1.0 |
| cost | $0.2882 cold · $0.0120/email · $0.0000 and 0 calls on re-run |

Treat those with suspicion. I iterated against this key five times; see *Predictions* below for
what I actually expect.

## The shape of it

**Code decides everything checkable; the model decides only what requires reading; nothing the
model says ships without being verified against the source.**

Code owns: MIME, the current-vs-quoted split, routing attachments by magic bytes, hidden
sheets, text-layer-vs-scan, the uom vocabulary, de-duplication, duplicate and revision links,
every `needs_review` rule, and the groundedness check. The model owns: which of seven classes,
which rows are items, and which context belongs on which line. Those are reading judgements and
no amount of regex does them.

Between the two sits the thing I'd defend first: **every extracted line's `raw` must actually
occur in the document it claims to come from**, by token coverage rather than substring (a
pasted spreadsheet splits one row across three lines, so substring is too strict). Lines that
fail are dropped. This is not theoretical — on E006 the call reading the 44-line PDF tried to
emit the two gasket lines that live in the email body, because the body is supplied as ambient
context. Code dropped them before they shipped. Precision is a property of the system, not a
hope about a prompt.

The second thing I'd defend: **quoted history is excluded from what the model sees**, not
merely labelled. E012 is a status inquiry with an entire seven-line RFQ pasted underneath;
nothing about it reaches the extractor, so there is no opportunity to hallucinate it, and the
groundedness check would drop it even if there were.

## Something in the data that surprised me

I assumed I could tell a company logo from a document by file size, and wrote the threshold
before looking. In E010 the Delta Mechanical logo is **3,307 bytes** and the screenshot of the
spreadsheet holding six real line items is **4,295**. In E017 the Cobalt Ridge logo is **5,288
bytes** — larger than both. Any byte threshold I would have picked silently deletes a
customer's order, and E017 is precisely the email where losing the attachment is the whole
point of the test.

So every image goes to the vision model and `"decorative"` is an answer it is allowed to give.
It costs about $0.002 to ask a model whether a 4KB PNG is a logo, which is the correct price
for not dropping an order. `looks_decorative()` survives only as a filename hint, used nowhere
that can delete a line.

The second surprise was mechanical. On E009's two-page phone scan, reading a whole page at once
got **13 of 28** quantities right; the same model reading three overlapping horizontal strips
of that same page got **28 of 28**. I assumed a stronger model would fix it and tested that:
`gpt-5` on the whole page scored **14 of 28** — no better than `gpt-4.1`. The failure is row
drift across a tall skewed table, not recognition, and it is fixed by showing fewer rows per
look, not by spending more.

## Something in the README I disagree with

> `needs_review` … Only for `rfq`, `rfq_revision` and `purchase_order`.

This makes the flag unavailable exactly when it is most needed. My resilience test generates an
email with an empty subject, an empty body and one corrupt attachment. There is no evidence of
what it is. The model called it `other` — a defensible reading of nothing — and the rule then
forbids flagging it, so it leaves with no lines and no flag. That is a textbook silent loss, the
failure the same document ranks as the most expensive, produced by following the format.

What I did: when nothing in an email could be read — empty body, every attachment unopenable —
and the headers do not positively say machine-generated (no bounce envelope, no
`Auto-Submitted`, no `List-Unsubscribe`), code overrides the class to `rfq` so the flag becomes
legal, and flags it. I am choosing a possible phantom request over a possible silent loss, on
the same asymmetry the brief sets out. If the grader counts that as a misclassification, I would
rather lose that point than the customer.

A smaller one: *"Not items in quoted earlier messages"* is right nine times in ten and wrong on
E020, where "go ahead with items 1, 2 and 4" names items that exist **only** in the quoted
quote. I kept the rule and gave it three declared exceptions, each detectable from the current
message alone: a message that selects numbered items from the history, one of our own reps
forwarding a customer, and a revision restating an order. Everything else sees no history at all.

## Predictions for the held-out inbox

Dev is saturated and I tuned against it, so I expect a real drop. My honest ranges for ~40
emails:

| | predicted |
|---|---|
| silent losses | **0–1** |
| hallucinated lines | 0–4 |
| lost / phantom requests | 0–2 |
| classification | 88–95% |
| line recall / precision | 93–98% / 96–99% |
| qty | 94–98% |
| context carried | 90–96% |
| `needs_review` recall | 0.85–1.0 |

**The two kinds I expect to get wrong.**

*Photographs and scans of dense tables.* Even after the strip fix, E009 still swaps the
quantities of items 11 and 12 — adjacent rows, 2 errors in 210 lines. That failure mode has not
gone away, it has shrunk. Handwriting worse than dev's, a steeper camera angle, a table with no
item-number column to anchor on, or a multi-column form will push it back up. It will show as
wrong `qty` on paired lines rather than as missing lines, which is the better way to be wrong,
but it is where my numbers will fall first.

*Thread messages that do two things at once.* The classifier picks one of seven labels for a
message that chases a quote **and** changes it, or commits to part of an order **and** asks a
question. Dev has one instance of each in isolation and I get both right; a message that mixes
them has no right answer in this schema and I will pick the wrong half. Related: a purchase
order that accepts items by description rather than by number ("go ahead with the flanges and
the pipe") — my `selects_items_from_quoted` path keys on labels it can name, and a prose
selection will either over- or under-select from the quote.

I also expect `vendor_quote` to be my most fragile class. Dev's example is unmistakable — it
quotes our own rep, with prices, lead times and FOB terms. A supplier email without those
tells, or a distributor who is both customer and supplier, would read as an `rfq` and become a
phantom request.

## How this runs for real

**3,000 emails a day by webhook.** The webhook does one thing: write the raw bytes to object
storage and push a job. Workers run the existing per-email phase A, which already shares
nothing between emails and is already thread-parallel. Phase B — duplicates, revisions, the
review flag — needs its thread's history, so it keys on a thread id and runs after, serialised
per thread rather than globally; that is the one piece of today's design that does not scale
as written, because `link_inbox` walks a list in memory. At 3,000/day and $0.012 that is $36 a
day, and the classification gate means the roughly 40% of a real inbox that carries no items
costs a twentieth of that. **Built:** the per-email isolation, the parallelism, the cost
accounting. **Not built:** the queue, the thread store.

and jitter. Past that the email returns flagged with the reason and the run continues — a
two-hour outage produces a backlog of flagged emails, not a crash and not an empty file. What

inbox slows to the timeout) and a requeue, so the flagged ones are retried when the provider
returns instead of waiting for a human. **Built:** retries, degradation, the never-crash
boundary — verified by running the whole dev inbox with the key removed. **Not built:** the
breaker and the requeue.

documents chunk at ~18k characters on line boundaries with the opening lines carried into each
chunk, because that is where the "unless noted" defaults live; scans go one call per page.
**Built**, though the cap is a blunt instrument — the right version prices the document first
and asks before spending $40 on one email.

**The same email delivered twice.** Two independent mechanisms. The cache is content-addressed,
so the second delivery makes zero model calls and costs nothing. The duplicate rule then marks
it: same sender, same subject once `Re:`/`FW:`/`RESEND:` are stripped, plus content equality by
attachment hash, body text, or extracted line set. E008 is byte-identical attachments under a
rewritten covering note, so the hash does the work there. **Built.**

## What I rejected

**A stronger model instead of better framing.** Measured, not assumed — `gpt-5` scored 14/28 on
the scan that strips fixed at 28/28.

**Defaulting to `gpt-5.x` because the key reached it.** You run the held-out inbox with your
key. If it lacks the model I named, the run dies. I default to models that are broadly
available and whose price I can state, and fall back rather than fail.

**One extraction call per email.** Per document gives correct `source` by construction, bounded
prompts, parallelism, and a failure that takes down one attachment instead of an inbox.

**Regex extraction for the "easy" plain-text emails.** E001 looks parseable until you notice
`4" 150# RF slip-on flange, A105 x 6` puts the quantity last, E002 says "a couple caps", and
E018 is a spreadsheet pasted into plain text with qty, description and size on three separate
lines. A second code path would need all the same judgement and would disagree with the first.

## What I know is broken

- Two quantities in E009 are still wrong (adjacent rows in a scanned table).

  against — so image-sourced lines ship on the model's word alone. That is where a
  hallucination would get through, and it is the gap I would close next.

- Item-number de-duplication only engages when the leading numbers look like a contiguous
  index. A strip-split table whose index restarts mid-document would keep a duplicate row.
- The classifier's second-opinion escalation has never fired on real data — it is tested only
  by construction, so I trust it least of anything here.

## What's next, in order

   extracted lines against it — closes the one place a hallucination can still ship.
2. A held-out-style regression set of my own: perturb the dev emails (re-skew the scans, rename
   headings, shuffle sections) and watch which numbers move. Dev at 100% tells me nothing more.
3. The queue, the circuit breaker and the requeue from the section above.
4. The matcher — designed in `MATCHER.md`, not built.

## Time

Roughly 9 hours, in one sitting, with Claude Code (see `AI_USAGE.md`). About half of that was
the two measurement loops — building the scorer, then the strip experiment — rather than
writing pipeline code.

| line recall / precision | 93–98% / 96–99% |
| qty | 94–98% |
| context carried | 90–96% |
| `needs_review` recall | 0.85–1.0 |

**The two kinds I expect to get wrong.**

*Photographs and scans of dense tables.* Even after the strip fix, E009 still swaps the
quantities of items 11 and 12 — adjacent rows, 2 errors in 210 lines. That failure mode has not
gone away, it has shrunk. Handwriting worse than dev's, a steeper camera angle, a table with no
item-number column to anchor on, or a multi-column form will push it back up. It will show as
wrong `qty` on paired lines rather than as missing lines, which is the better way to be wrong,
but it is where my numbers will fall first.

*Thread messages that do two things at once.* The classifier picks one of seven labels for a
message that chases a quote **and** changes it, or commits to part of an order **and** asks a
question. Dev has one instance of each in isolation and I get both right; a message that mixes
them has no right answer in this schema and I will pick the wrong half. Related: a purchase
order that accepts items by description rather than by number ("go ahead with the flanges and
the pipe") — my `selects_items_from_quoted` path keys on labels it can name, and a prose
selection will either over- or under-select from the quote.

I also expect `vendor_quote` to be my most fragile class. Dev's example is unmistakable — it
quotes our own rep, with prices, lead times and FOB terms. A supplier email without those
tells, or a distributor who is both customer and supplier, would read as an `rfq` and become a
phantom request.

## How this runs for real

**3,000 emails a day by webhook.** The webhook does one thing: write the raw bytes to object
storage and push a job. Workers run the existing per-email phase A, which already shares
nothing between emails and is already thread-parallel. Phase B — duplicates, revisions, the
review flag — needs its thread's history, so it keys on a thread id and runs after, serialised
per thread rather than globally; that is the one piece of today's design that does not scale
as written, because `link_inbox` walks a list in memory. At 3,000/day and $0.012 that is $36 a
day, and the classification gate means the roughly 40% of a real inbox that carries no items
costs a twentieth of that. **Built:** the per-email isolation, the parallelism, the cost
accounting. **Not built:** the queue, the thread store.

**The provider is down for two hours.** Each call retries four times with exponential backoff
and jitter. Past that the email returns flagged with the reason and the run continues — a
two-hour outage produces a backlog of flagged emails, not a crash and not an empty file. What
is missing is a circuit breaker (right now every email pays its own four retries, so the whole
inbox slows to the timeout) and a requeue, so the flagged ones are retried when the provider
returns instead of waiting for a human. **Built:** retries, degradation, the never-crash
boundary — verified by running the whole dev inbox with the key removed. **Not built:** the
breaker and the requeue.

**A 300-page PDF.** Capped at 20 pages (`DEFAULT_PAGE_CAP`), and a document that was truncated
sets `needs_review` naming the file, so nobody quotes two thirds of a job without knowing. Text
documents chunk at ~18k characters on line boundaries with the opening lines carried into each
chunk, because that is where the "unless noted" defaults live; scans go one call per page.
**Built**, though the cap is a blunt instrument — the right version prices the document first
and asks before spending $40 on one email.

**The same email delivered twice.** Two independent mechanisms. The cache is content-addressed,
so the second delivery makes zero model calls and costs nothing. The duplicate rule then marks
it: same sender, same subject once `Re:`/`FW:`/`RESEND:` are stripped, plus content equality by
attachment hash, body text, or extracted line set. E008 is byte-identical attachments under a
rewritten covering note, so the hash does the work there. **Built.**

## What I rejected

**A stronger model instead of better framing.** Measured, not assumed — `gpt-5` scored 14/28 on
the scan that strips fixed at 28/28.

**Defaulting to `gpt-5.x` because the key reached it.** You run the held-out inbox with your
key. If it lacks the model I named, the run dies. I default to models that are broadly
available and whose price I can state, and fall back rather than fail.

**One extraction call per email.** Per document gives correct `source` by construction, bounded
prompts, parallelism, and a failure that takes down one attachment instead of an inbox.

**Regex extraction for the "easy" plain-text emails.** E001 looks parseable until you notice
`4" 150# RF slip-on flange, A105 x 6` puts the quantity last, E002 says "a couple caps", and
E018 is a spreadsheet pasted into plain text with qty, description and size on three separate
lines. A second code path would need all the same judgement and would disagree with the first.

## What I know is broken

- Two quantities in E009 are still wrong (adjacent rows in a scanned table).
- `verify.py` cannot ground a line that came from a picture — there is no text to check it
  against — so image-sourced lines ship on the model's word alone. That is where a
  hallucination would get through, and it is the gap I would close next.
- `link_inbox` holds the inbox in memory; fine for 40 emails, wrong for a live queue.
- Item-number de-duplication only engages when the leading numbers look like a contiguous
  index. A strip-split table whose index restarts mid-document would keep a duplicate row.
- The classifier's second-opinion escalation has never fired on real data — it is tested only
  by construction, so I trust it least of anything here.

## What's next, in order

1. Ground image-sourced lines by asking for a verbatim transcription pass and checking the
   extracted lines against it — closes the one place a hallucination can still ship.
2. A held-out-style regression set of my own: perturb the dev emails (re-skew the scans, rename
   headings, shuffle sections) and watch which numbers move. Dev at 100% tells me nothing more.
3. The queue, the circuit breaker and the requeue from the section above.
4. The matcher — designed in `MATCHER.md`, not built.

## Time

Roughly 9 hours, in one sitting, with Claude Code (see `AI_USAGE.md`). About half of that was
the two measurement loops — building the scorer, then the strip experiment — rather than
writing pipeline code.

# AI usage

> The raw transcript is in `ai-sessions/`. It contains the OpenAI key from the assessment
> email, pasted into the session before I thought about it; it is redacted there.

## Setup

**Claude Code** (CLI, Opus 5, 1M context) for all of it — one session, no subagents, no MCP
servers, no custom skills, no `CLAUDE.md`. Everything the agent knew about this problem it
read out of `ASSESSMENT.md`, `data/README.md`, the 24 `.eml` files and `answer_key.json` at
the start of the session.

That was deliberate. The failure mode I was worried about was an agent confidently writing a
parser for emails it had never opened, so the first instruction was to read the whole package
and explain the problem back to me before proposing anything, and the second was to design the
architecture in prose before writing a line of code. Both of those outputs are in the
transcript ahead of the first file.

The one piece of tooling that mattered is not an agent feature at all: `scripts/score.py`,
written early, implementing the brief's metrics in the order it says it grades them. After
that existed, every change was judged by a number instead of by whether the diff looked
reasonable.

## How I worked

Deterministic layer first and verified with no model at all — all 24 emails ingested, every
attachment routed, the hidden Excel sheet skipped, the encrypted PDF flagged — so that when
model answers started arriving I knew the inputs were right. Then the scorer, then the model
layer. From there it was a loop: run, score, read the per-email diff, find the *cause* rather
than patch the symptom, fix, re-run. Five of those loops took dev from P 70.6% / 87 hallucinated
lines to P/R 100% with none.

I reviewed every diff. Two rules I kept to: a fix goes in the layer that owns the decision
(vague quantities became a code rule in `verify.py`, not another sentence in a prompt), and no
fix may name a string from the dev set — rules are about phenomena (hidden sheets, superseded
revisions, decorative images, bounce envelopes) because the held-out inbox has the same
situations in different words.

## Three moments

**It was wrong, and the scorer caught it — `0d8363a`.** Splitting tall scans into overlapping
strips fixed the quantity errors, so the agent added de-duplication by item number to remove
rows that appear in two strips. The next score run showed line recall had *fallen*: E010 lost
`40 | EA | 1/2"-13 hex nut, zinc`. That screenshot's first column is the quantity, not an item
number, and two different rows legitimately want 40 of something — so "duplicate item number"
had deleted a real line. The fix was to check whether the leading numbers form a contiguous
index before trusting them. I would not have found this by reading the diff; a net-positive
change hid a regression inside it, and only a per-line comparison against the key surfaced it.
This is the single strongest argument for having written the scorer first.

**I overruled it — `928bd5c` / `RUNNING.md`.** The key reached `gpt-5`, `gpt-5.4`, `gpt-5.5`
and more, and the obvious move was to default to the newest thing available. I said no, for a
reason that has nothing to do with quality: *they* run the held-out inbox with *their* key, and
if it cannot reach the model I named, the run dies. Defaults are pinned to the `gpt-4.1` family
— broadly available, and prices I can actually state in a cost report — with a fallback chain
for keys that cannot reach even those. The agent then tested the assumption I had implicitly
made, which was the better half of the exchange: on the scanned table that was failing,
`gpt-5` scored 14/28 and `gpt-4.1` scored 13/28. The newer model would have cost more, risked
the run, and fixed nothing.

**It saved me real time — `0d8363a`.** Ten quantities were wrong on E009's phone scan and I
would have spent an hour on image preprocessing — deskewing, upscaling, contrast. Instead the
agent proposed measuring four strategies against the answer key before changing anything:
full page, three overlapping strips, and two other models. That experiment took about four
minutes and returned an unambiguous answer (13/28 vs 28/28 vs 14/28) which both identified the
real mechanism — row drift over a tall table, not recognition — and ruled out the two
approaches I would have tried first.

**One more worth recording, because it is the test rather than the agent.** The resilience
inbox in `tests/test_resilience.py` failed on its first run, on a case neither of us had
designed for: an email with an empty subject, an empty body and one corrupt attachment comes
back classified `other`, and the output format forbids `needs_review` on `other`, so it leaves
with no lines and no flag. A silent loss produced by following the spec. That is now a code
override and it is written up in `DECISIONS.md` as my disagreement with the README. The agent
wrote the test; the test found the bug; neither the agent nor I had reasoned our way to it.

# The matcher — designed, not built

Each extracted line has to become a catalog part, or a decision that Ridgeline doesn't stock
it. I did not build this; here is how I would, and why it is shaped the way it is.

## The shape the catalog hands you

`catalog.csv` is not a list of descriptions — it is already a structured table:
`category, product, size, spec, material, ends, extra, uom`, with 937 rows over 7 categories
and a closed vocabulary in every column (12 `ends` values, 22 `spec` values, `extra` is one of
nine). `description` is just an ERP rendering of those columns.

That settles the approach. **This is not a text-similarity problem.** Fuzzy-matching a
customer's sentence against an abbreviated ERP description is exactly how you quote the wrong
part, because the nearest string is routinely one attribute away from the right one. The job is
to parse the customer's free text into the *same schema the catalog already uses*, then compare
attributes exactly.

## The decision

1. **Normalise the line into catalog attributes.** From `description` (which the parser has
   already made self-contained) produce `{category, product, size, spec, material, ends, extra}`,
   using each column's own vocabulary — `Schedule 40`→`SCH 40`, `150 lb`/`Class 150`→`150#`,
   `butt weld`→`BW`, `threaded`/`NPT`→`THD`, `seamless`→`SMLS`, `1 1/2"`→`1-1/2`. Leave an
   attribute **absent** when the customer didn't state it. Absent is not a wildcard-with-a-guess;
   it is information about what they didn't pin down.

2. **Generate candidates** by exact index on `(product, size)` — a dictionary lookup, no
   scoring. `2" 90 elbow` gives 14 rows. Product names come from a synonym map onto the
   catalog's own `product` column (`ell`→`90 elbow`, `SPW`→`spiral wound gasket`, `WN`→`weld
   neck flange`, `T&C`→ends, not product).

3. **Filter by every attribute the customer DID state.** A stated attribute must agree exactly.
   Nothing is rounded, substituted or taken as "close enough".

4. **Decide by how many rows survive:**
   - exactly one → `matched`, that sku
   - more than one → `ambiguous`, `sku: null`, survivors in `candidates`
   - none → `not_in_catalog`, `sku: null`

The whole design is in step 4's symmetry: **silence widens the candidate set; it never narrows
it.** `1" WN 150# RF` names no material, and the catalog holds exactly one 1" 150# RF weld neck
(`RL-26367`, A105) — one survivor, so it matches, correctly, without anyone guessing a material.
Ask for `2" ball valve, threaded` and five rows survive on port and WOG rating and body
material; that is genuinely a question for the customer, not a coin flip.

## Why not-in-catalog has to be a real answer

Every one of the 16 non-matched lines in the dev key is one attribute away from something we
stock, which is exactly what makes substitution tempting and wrong:

| the customer asked for | what we stock | if you substituted |
|---|---|---|
| 14" weld neck flange, **150#** | 14" weld neck only in **300#** | wrong pressure class |
| 2" spiral wound, **316**/graphite, 300# | same size and class in **304** | wrong gasket material |
| 2" ball valve, **bronze, 125#** | 2" ball only in 304/316 SS at WOG ratings | wrong material and rating |
| **5/8" x 3-1/4"** B7 stud | 5/8" x 3" and 5/8" x **3-1/2"** | bolt that doesn't fit the flange |
| **eccentric** reducer 6" x 4" | **concentric** reducer only | wrong geometry for the line |
| **half** coupling 2" | full coupling only | wrong part |
| Y-strainer, hex head plug | not carried at all | — |

Three of those (material, class, length) would pass any string-similarity threshold loose
enough to be useful. So: no fallback, no "nearest part", no confidence score that lets a near
miss through. A `not_in_catalog` costs a buyer a phone call; a confident wrong sku costs a
rebuild.

## Where the model helps, and what it must never do

The model does **step 1 only** — reading a customer's prose into the attribute schema, which is
the same context-carrying judgement the parser already does well. It returns attributes, with
each one marked stated or absent.

The model never sees the catalog, never ranks candidates, and never names a sku. Steps 2–4 are
a dictionary lookup and a set intersection: deterministic, auditable, instantly re-runnable
when the catalog changes, and incapable of inventing `RL-31415`. If a model picks the part, a
wrong pick is unexplainable and unreproducible; if code picks it, `match_reason` writes itself —
*"2" 3000# A105 THD 90 elbow: one part fits"*, or *"14" weld neck 150#: we stock 14" weld neck
only in 300#"*.

One place I would let the model back in, read-only: when zero rows survive, ask it to name
*which attribute* caused it, so the reason line is useful to a rep. Its answer goes in the text,
never in the decision.

## How I'd measure it

The brief grades confident wrong matches first, so that is the headline: **a line where we named
a sku and the key says a different sku, `not_in_catalog`, or `ambiguous`.** Target zero; it is
the only matcher error that reaches a customer as a wrong quote. Then `not_in_catalog` recall
(of the 16 the key marks, how many did we decline to match), then plain accuracy, and
separately the `ambiguous` split — because the failure mode of a cautious matcher is flooding
reps with questions, and `ambiguous` on something a rep would call obvious is a real cost even
though the brief doesn't score it.

`scripts/score.py` already pairs our lines to the key's, so adding the matcher's three numbers
is a small extension of the same loop.

Two things I would watch on held-out data. Dev contains **no `ambiguous` lines at all** —
194 matched, 16 not-in-catalog — so my ambiguity rule is entirely untested and is the part most
likely to be wrong. And matching inherits every parser error upstream: a description missing its
schedule because a heading didn't carry becomes an ambiguity or a miss here, so matcher accuracy
is bounded above by the "context carried" number in `DECISIONS.md` and should be read alongside
it, never on its own.

"""The command.

    parse --emails <dir> --out parsed.json

Exit codes: 0 the run completed (flagged emails are a normal outcome, not a
failure), 2 the run completed but some emails could not reach a model, 1 the
run could not start at all.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import json
import os
import sys
from pathlib import Path

from .pipeline import DEFAULT_CLASSIFY_MODEL, DEFAULT_EXTRACT_MODEL, DEFAULT_VISION_MODEL, run

REPO = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent


def _load_dotenv() -> None:
    """Read OPENAI_API_KEY from a .env beside the repo if the environment has none."""
    if os.getenv("OPENAI_API_KEY"):
        return
    env = REPO / ".env"
    if not env.exists():
        return
    for line in env.read_text(encoding="utf-8", errors="replace").splitlines():
        line = line.strip()
        if not line or line.startswith("#") or "=" not in line:
            continue
        k, v = line.split("=", 1)
        os.environ.setdefault(k.strip(), v.strip().strip("'\""))


def build_parser() -> argparse.ArgumentParser:
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser(prog="rfq", description=__doc__)
    sub = ap.add_subparsers(dest="command", required=True)

    p = sub.add_parser("parse", help="read an inbox of .eml files into parsed.json")
    p.add_argument("--emails", type=Path, required=True, help="directory of .eml files")
    p.add_argument("--out", type=Path, required=True, help="where to write parsed.json")
    p.add_argument("--cache", type=Path, default=REPO / "cache", help="recorded model answers")
    p.add_argument("--cost-report", type=Path, default=None, help="where to write the cost summary")
    p.add_argument("--traces", type=Path, default=None, help="directory for per-email traces")
    p.add_argument("--concurrency", type=int, default=6)
    p.add_argument("--refresh", action="store_true", help="ignore the cache and call the model again")
    p.add_argument("--no-cache-write", action="store_true", help="do not record new answers")
    p.add_argument("--model-classify", default=DEFAULT_CLASSIFY_MODEL)
    p.add_argument("--model-extract", default=DEFAULT_EXTRACT_MODEL)
    p.add_argument("--model-vision", default=DEFAULT_VISION_MODEL)
    p.add_argument("--quiet", action="store_true")
    return ap


def main(argv: list[str] | None = None) -> int:
    args = build_parser().parse_args(argv)
    if args.command != "parse":  # pragma: no cover
        return 1

    _load_dotenv()
    if not args.emails.is_dir():
        print(f"--emails: {args.emails} is not a directory", file=sys.stderr)
        return 1

    parsed, cost, results = run(
        args.emails,
        cache_dir=args.cache,
        api_key=os.getenv("OPENAI_API_KEY"),
        models={
            "classify": args.model_classify,
            "extract": args.model_extract,
            "vision": args.model_vision,
        },
        concurrency=max(1, args.concurrency),
        refresh=args.refresh,
        write_cache=not args.no_cache_write,
    )

    args.out.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    args.out.write_text(json.dumps(parsed, indent=2, ensure_ascii=False) + "\n", encoding="utf-8")

    report = args.cost_report or args.out.with_name(args.out.stem + ".cost.json")
    report.write_text(json.dumps(cost, indent=2, ensure_ascii=False) + "\n", encoding="utf-8")

    if args.traces:
        args.traces.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        for r in results:
            (args.traces / f"{r.id}.json").write_text(
                json.dumps(r.trace(), indent=2, ensure_ascii=False, default=str) + "\n", encoding="utf-8"
            )

    degraded = [r.id for r in results if r.errors]
    if not args.quiet:
        flagged = [r.id for r in results if r.needs_review]
        lines = sum(len(v["line_items"]) for v in parsed.values())
        print(f"{len(parsed)} emails -> {args.out}  ({lines} line items)")
        cold = cost["cold_run"]
        print(
            f"  model calls {cost['model_calls']}, cache hits {cost['cache_hits']}, "
            f"${cost['cost_usd']:.4f} spent this run"
            + ("  [replayed from cache, no API key]" if cost["offline_replay"] else "")
        )
        print(
            f"  cold run would be {cold['prompt_tokens']:,} in / {cold['completion_tokens']:,} out tokens, "
            f"${cold['cost_usd']:.4f} (${cold['cost_per_email_usd']:.5f}/email)"
        )
        print(f"  needs_review: {len(flagged)}" + (f" ({', '.join(flagged)})" if flagged else ""))
        if degraded:
            print(f"  degraded (could not reach a model): {', '.join(degraded)}", file=sys.stderr)
        print(f"  cost report -> {report}")
    return 2 if degraded else 0

"""The command.

    parse --emails <dir> --out parsed.json

Exit codes: 0 the run completed (flagged emails are a normal outcome, not a
failure), 2 the run completed but some emails could not reach a model, 1 the
run could not start at all.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import json
import os
import sys
from pathlib import Path

from .pipeline import DEFAULT_CLASSIFY_MODEL, DEFAULT_EXTRACT_MODEL, DEFAULT_VISION_MODEL, run

REPO = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent


def default_cache() -> Path:
    """Where the recorded answers live.

    Installed with `pip install -e .` the package sits in the repo and REPO is right.
    Installed without -e it sits in site-packages, where there is no cache — so the
    working directory wins when it has one.  Getting this wrong silently turns a
    keyless replay into 'no recorded answer for this input' on every email.
    """
    for candidate in (Path.cwd() / "cache", REPO / "cache"):
        if candidate.is_dir():
            return candidate
    return Path.cwd() / "cache"


def _load_dotenv() -> None:
    """Read OPENAI_API_KEY from a .env beside the repo if the environment has none."""
    if os.getenv("OPENAI_API_KEY"):
        return
    env = REPO / ".env"
    if not env.exists():
        return
    for line in env.read_text(encoding="utf-8", errors="replace").splitlines():
        line = line.strip()
        if not line or line.startswith("#") or "=" not in line:
            continue
        k, v = line.split("=", 1)
        os.environ.setdefault(k.strip(), v.strip().strip("'\""))


def build_parser() -> argparse.ArgumentParser:
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser(prog="rfq", description=__doc__)
    sub = ap.add_subparsers(dest="command", required=True)

    p = sub.add_parser("parse", help="read an inbox of .eml files into parsed.json")
    p.add_argument("--emails", type=Path, required=True, help="directory of .eml files")
    p.add_argument("--out", type=Path, required=True, help="where to write parsed.json")
    p.add_argument("--cache", type=Path, default=None, help="recorded model answers (default: ./cache, else the repo's)")
    p.add_argument("--cost-report", type=Path, default=None, help="where to write the cost summary")
    p.add_argument("--traces", type=Path, default=None, help="directory for per-email traces")
    p.add_argument("--concurrency", type=int, default=6)
    p.add_argument("--refresh", action="store_true", help="ignore the cache and call the model again")
    p.add_argument("--no-cache-write", action="store_true", help="do not record new answers")
    p.add_argument("--model-classify", default=DEFAULT_CLASSIFY_MODEL)
    p.add_argument("--model-extract", default=DEFAULT_EXTRACT_MODEL)
    p.add_argument("--model-vision", default=DEFAULT_VISION_MODEL)
    p.add_argument("--quiet", action="store_true")
    return ap


def main(argv: list[str] | None = None) -> int:
    args = build_parser().parse_args(argv)
    if args.command != "parse":  # pragma: no cover
        return 1

    _load_dotenv()
    if not args.emails.is_dir():
        print(f"--emails: {args.emails} is not a directory", file=sys.stderr)
        return 1

    parsed, cost, results = run(
        args.emails,
        cache_dir=args.cache or default_cache(),
        api_key=os.getenv("OPENAI_API_KEY"),
        models={
            "classify": args.model_classify,
            "extract": args.model_extract,
            "vision": args.model_vision,
        },
        concurrency=max(1, args.concurrency),
        refresh=args.refresh,
        write_cache=not args.no_cache_write,
    )

    args.out.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    args.out.write_text(json.dumps(parsed, indent=2, ensure_ascii=False) + "\n", encoding="utf-8")

    report = args.cost_report or args.out.with_name(args.out.stem + ".cost.json")
    report.write_text(json.dumps(cost, indent=2, ensure_ascii=False) + "\n", encoding="utf-8")

    if args.traces:
        args.traces.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        for r in results:
            (args.traces / f"{r.id}.json").write_text(
                json.dumps(r.trace(), indent=2, ensure_ascii=False, default=str) + "\n", encoding="utf-8"
            )

    degraded = [r.id for r in results if r.errors]
    if not args.quiet:
        flagged = [r.id for r in results if r.needs_review]
        lines = sum(len(v["line_items"]) for v in parsed.values())
        print(f"{len(parsed)} emails -> {args.out}  ({lines} line items)")
        cold = cost["cold_run"]
        print(
            f"  model calls {cost['model_calls']}, cache hits {cost['cache_hits']}, "
            f"${cost['cost_usd']:.4f} spent this run"
            + ("  [replayed from cache, no API key]" if cost["offline_replay"] else "")
        )
        print(
            f"  cold run would be {cold['prompt_tokens']:,} in / {cold['completion_tokens']:,} out tokens, "
            f"${cold['cost_usd']:.4f} (${cold['cost_per_email_usd']:.5f}/email)"
        )
        print(f"  needs_review: {len(flagged)}" + (f" ({', '.join(flagged)})" if flagged else ""))
        if degraded:
            print(f"  degraded (could not reach a model): {', '.join(degraded)}", file=sys.stderr)
        print(f"  cost report -> {report}")
    return 2 if degraded else 0

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Copy this project's Claude Code transcripts into ai-sessions/, with keys redacted.

Run it LAST, just before sending — the session file keeps growing while you work.

    python scripts/export_sessions.py

It copies every .jsonl under ~/.claude/projects/<this-project>/ and replaces anything
that looks like an API key.  It then re-scans the output and refuses to finish if a
key-shaped string survived, so the check is not a matter of trusting the regex.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import re
import shutil
import sys
from pathlib import Path

REPO = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
OUT = REPO / "ai-sessions"

# OpenAI (sk-..., sk-proj-...), Anthropic (sk-ant-...), AWS, generic bearer tokens
PATTERNS = [
    (re.compile(r"sk-(?:proj-|ant-|live-|test-)?[A-Za-z0-9_\-]{16,}"), "[REDACTED-API-KEY]"),
    (re.compile(r"\bAKIA[0-9A-Z]{16}\b"), "[REDACTED-AWS-KEY]"),
    (re.compile(r"\bgh[pousr]_[A-Za-z0-9]{20,}\b"), "[REDACTED-GITHUB-TOKEN]"),
    (re.compile(r"(?i)\b(bearer)\s+[A-Za-z0-9._\-]{24,}"), r"\1 [REDACTED-TOKEN]"),
]
# anything key-shaped that must not survive the pass
LEFTOVER = re.compile(r"sk-[A-Za-z0-9_\-]{16,}|AKIA[0-9A-Z]{16}|gh[pousr]_[A-Za-z0-9]{20,}")


def project_dir() -> Path:
    slug = str(REPO).replace("/", "-")
    return Path.home() / ".claude" / "projects" / slug


def main() -> int:
    src = project_dir()
    if not src.is_dir():
        print(f"no session directory at {src}", file=sys.stderr)
        print("if your tool cannot export, say so in AI_USAGE.md and bring the history to the interview.")
        return 1

    OUT.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    files = sorted(src.glob("*.jsonl"))
    if not files:
        print(f"no .jsonl transcripts in {src}", file=sys.stderr)
        return 1

    redactions = 0
    for f in files:
        text = f.read_text(encoding="utf-8", errors="replace")
        for pat, repl in PATTERNS:
            text, n = pat.subn(repl, text)
            redactions += n
        dest = OUT / f.name
        dest.write_text(text, encoding="utf-8")
        print(f"  {f.name}  {len(text) / 1_000_000:.1f} MB")

    # verify, rather than assume, that nothing key-shaped survived
    survivors = []
    for dest in OUT.glob("*.jsonl"):
        for i, line in enumerate(dest.read_text(encoding="utf-8", errors="replace").splitlines(), 1):
            if LEFTOVER.search(line):
                survivors.append(f"{dest.name}:{i}")

    print(f"\n{len(files)} transcript(s) -> {OUT}")
    print(f"{redactions} secret(s) redacted")

    if survivors:
        print("\nREFUSING TO FINISH — key-shaped strings survived redaction:", file=sys.stderr)
        for s in survivors[:20]:
            print(f"  {s}", file=sys.stderr)
        for dest in OUT.glob("*.jsonl"):
            dest.unlink()
        print("output deleted; fix the patterns and re-run.", file=sys.stderr)
        return 1

    print("verified: no key-shaped strings remain")
    print("\nalso check by hand:  grep -R 'sk-' ai-sessions/ | head")
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Copy this project's Claude Code transcripts into ai-sessions/, with keys redacted.

Run it LAST, just before sending — the session file keeps growing while you work.

    python scripts/export_sessions.py

It copies every .jsonl under ~/.claude/projects/<this-project>/ and replaces anything
that looks like an API key.  It then re-scans the output and refuses to finish if a
key-shaped string survived, so the check is not a matter of trusting the regex.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import re
import shutil
import sys
from pathlib import Path

REPO = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
OUT = REPO / "ai-sessions"

# OpenAI (sk-..., sk-proj-...), Anthropic (sk-ant-...), AWS, generic bearer tokens
PATTERNS = [
    (re.compile(r"sk-(?:proj-|ant-|live-|test-)?[A-Za-z0-9_\-]{16,}"), "[REDACTED-API-KEY]"),
    (re.compile(r"\bAKIA[0-9A-Z]{16}\b"), "[REDACTED-AWS-KEY]"),
    (re.compile(r"\bgh[pousr]_[A-Za-z0-9]{20,}\b"), "[REDACTED-GITHUB-TOKEN]"),
    (re.compile(r"(?i)\b(bearer)\s+[A-Za-z0-9._\-]{24,}"), r"\1 [REDACTED-TOKEN]"),
]
# anything key-shaped that must not survive the pass
LEFTOVER = re.compile(r"sk-[A-Za-z0-9_\-]{16,}|AKIA[0-9A-Z]{16}|gh[pousr]_[A-Za-z0-9]{20,}")


def project_dir() -> Path:
    slug = str(REPO).replace("/", "-")
    return Path.home() / ".claude" / "projects" / slug


def main() -> int:
    src = project_dir()
    if not src.is_dir():
        print(f"no session directory at {src}", file=sys.stderr)
        print("if your tool cannot export, say so in AI_USAGE.md and bring the history to the interview.")
        return 1

    OUT.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    files = sorted(src.glob("*.jsonl"))
    if not files:
        print(f"no .jsonl transcripts in {src}", file=sys.stderr)
        return 1

    redactions = 0
    for f in files:
        text = f.read_text(encoding="utf-8", errors="replace")
        for pat, repl in PATTERNS:
            text, n = pat.subn(repl, text)
            redactions += n
        dest = OUT / f.name
        dest.write_text(text, encoding="utf-8")
        print(f"  {f.name}  {len(text) / 1_000_000:.1f} MB")

    # verify, rather than assume, that nothing key-shaped survived
    survivors = []
    for dest in OUT.glob("*.jsonl"):
        for i, line in enumerate(dest.read_text(encoding="utf-8", errors="replace").splitlines(), 1):
            if LEFTOVER.search(line):
                survivors.append(f"{dest.name}:{i}")

    print(f"\n{len(files)} transcript(s) -> {OUT}")
    print(f"{redactions} secret(s) redacted")

    if survivors:
        print("\nREFUSING TO FINISH — key-shaped strings survived redaction:", file=sys.stderr)
        for s in survivors[:20]:
            print(f"  {s}", file=sys.stderr)
        for dest in OUT.glob("*.jsonl"):
            dest.unlink()
        print("output deleted; fix the patterns and re-run.", file=sys.stderr)
        return 1

    print("verified: no key-shaped strings remain")
    print("\nalso check by hand:  grep -R 'sk-' ai-sessions/ | head")
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())
